subject: literature
passage: For eleven summers Mr. Dawlish and his neighbor Mrs. Pryce had each grown roses along the fence that divided their gardens, and for eleven summers each had pretended not to look at the other's. Mr. Dawlish pruned by the almanac; Mrs. Pryce pruned by instinct, and said so. When the frost that spring blackened his young shoots and spared hers, Mr. Dawlish bore it for a week. Then one evening, with the air of a man paying a debt, he leaned across the fence and asked what she had done. Mrs. Pryce, who had waited eleven years for the question, told him everything, and found she rather missed the silence.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A long, unspoken rivalry between two gardeners ends when one finally asks the other for advice.
choices.B: Mr. Dawlish's roses are damaged by a late frost that his neighbor's roses escape.
choices.C: Mrs. Pryce's roses survive the frost because she follows the almanac more carefully than Mr. Dawlish.
choices.D: Mr. Dawlish and Mrs. Pryce become close friends after years of refusing to speak to each other.

explanation.why: The text establishes an eleven-year rivalry in which each neighbor "pretended not to look at the other's" roses. The frost forces Mr. Dawlish to ask Mrs. Pryce what she did, and she tells him. The main idea is the ending of this silent competition, with a touch of irony in Mrs. Pryce missing the silence.
explanation.A: Correct. This covers the setup (years of silent rivalry) and the turn (Mr. Dawlish asking, Mrs. Pryce answering).
explanation.B: Incorrect. The frost is the event that prompts the question, but it is a detail, not the point of the whole text.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says Mrs. Pryce prunes by instinct, while Mr. Dawlish is the one who follows the almanac.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text describes one exchange of advice; it does not say they become close friends, and Mrs. Pryce even misses the silence.
